findings.title: Unauthenticated log injection through the password-reset form field
findings.evidence: ckan/views/user.py:612 reads the value straight off the request body: `id = request.form.get(u'user')`. Four lines later, with no neutralisation of any kind, ckan/views/user.py:616 writes it into the log: `log.info(u'Password reset requested for user "{}"'.format(id))`. The same value reaches a second sink at ckan/views/user.py:650-651: `log.info(u'User requested reset link for unknown user: {}'.format(id))`. The endpoint needs no credential: its gate is `logic.check_access(u'request_reset', context)` (ckan/views/user.py:606) and the auth function it resolves to is ckan/logic/auth/get.py:409-410, whose entire body is `return {'success': True}`. The shipped log format is line-oriented plain text that emits %(message)s raw - ckan/config/deployment.ini_tmpl:258: `format = %(asctime)s %(levelname)-5.5s [%(name)s] %(message)s` (identical in test-core.ini). A POST body field is not constrained by the HTTP header grammar, so CR and LF pass through intact.
findings.impact: Any anonymous client can append arbitrary, well-formed records to the application log by POSTing a `user` field containing CRLF followed by a fabricated line. Because the record is emitted by ckan.views.user at INFO, the forged line can impersonate any component and level - for example a fabricated `Emailing reset link to user: admin` - which destroys the accountability value of the log exactly where a password-reset incident would be reconstructed. Where the log is shipped to a line-parsing aggregator or rendered in a web log viewer, the same input reaches the parser or the page as content nobody wrote.
findings.recommendation: Neutralise control characters before the value reaches the logger, at the point of use rather than globally: log a repr (`%r`) so CR/LF are escaped, or strip/encode [\r\n\x00-\x1f] from `id` at ckan/views/user.py:612 before either sink. The durable fix is to emit structured (JSON-per-event) log records and to have the consumer parse that format - name both, since one without the other is not the exculpation.
findings.preconditions: None. Unauthenticated, single POST to /user/reset.
findings.verification: Call the handler with `user` = 'a\r\n2026-08-25 INFO  [ckan.views.user] Emailing reset link to user: admin' and count the lines the log gains. One input producing two records is the finding.

triage.FP-01: DOES_NOT_HOLD - no neutralising layer sits between request.form and the logger
triage.FP-02: DOES_NOT_HOLD - the value is a raw POST field with no validator between read and sink
triage.FP-03: DOES_NOT_HOLD - the shipped formatter (deployment.ini_tmpl:258) is line-oriented and does not escape control characters
triage.FP-10: DOES_NOT_HOLD - accountability loss is the impact, and it is real

findings.title: API key and bearer token written to the log in cleartext on every authenticated request
findings.evidence: ckan/views/__init__.py:260-282 collects the credential from the X-CKAN-API-Key header, the WSGI environ, or the Authorization header (lines 263-271), and then at line 277 writes the raw value to the log: `log.debug(u'Received API Key: %s' % apikey)`. Line 279-282 shows the value is a live credential: it is matched against `model.User.apikey` and, failing that, passed to `api_token.get_user_from_token(apikey)`. The log call happens before any validation, so both valid and invalid credentials are recorded. The formatter at ckan/config/deployment.ini_tmpl:258 emits the message verbatim; there is no redaction filter anywhere in the tree (no `filter_parameters`-equivalent processor exists - grep over ckan/ returns none).
findings.impact: Whoever can read the application log holds every API key and API token presented while DEBUG was enabled - operators, anyone with shell on the host, any log-shipping or error-tracking destination, and any backup of those logs. CKAN API keys are long-lived bearer credentials that carry the full authority of their user, including sysadmin, so this is a direct privilege-escalation path from log read to account takeover. It also widens the blast radius of any unrelated log-disclosure defect.
findings.recommendation: Delete the value from the message. If a breadcrumb is needed, log only a non-reversible fingerprint of the credential (a truncated HMAC) or the resolved user name after a successful lookup, never the presented secret. Add a redaction processor to the logging configuration so the class cannot reappear.
findings.preconditions: The `ckan` logger at DEBUG. The shipped deployment template sets `level = WARN` for the ckan logger, but DEBUG is a routine operational setting (ckan.debug) and the code offers no protection at any level once it is on.
findings.verification: Set the ckan logger to DEBUG, issue one request bearing a synthetic API key, and grep the log for that key. Appearing at all is the finding.

triage.FP-01: DOES_NOT_HOLD - no redaction filter exists in the tree
triage.FP-02: NOT_APPLICABLE - this is disclosure out through the log, not injection in
triage.FP-04: DOES_NOT_HOLD - the line is in the shipped view module, not behind a build or test flag; only the log level gates it
triage.FP-07: DOES_NOT_HOLD - an authentication credential has security value by definition

findings.title: Complete API request body logged at DEBUG, including passwords and tokens submitted to the action API
findings.evidence: ckan/views/api.py:220 logs the fully assembled request payload for every action-API call: `log.debug(u'Request data extracted: %r', request_data)`. The dict it prints is built at lines 184-219 from request.form, request.args, the JSON body and request.files, with no field filtering. Since /api/action/<logic_function> is the single entry point for every action (routes at ckan/views/api.py:509-514), the payloads passing through this line include `user_create` and `user_update` with the `password` field (schema at ckan/logic/schema.py, password accepted as free text) and `user_reset`. The legacy Pylons stack carries the same defect three times over and more broadly: ckan/controllers/api.py:373-375 logs request.params, request.POST and request.GET, :406 logs request.body, and :430 repeats the extracted dict. No sensitive-field filter exists anywhere in the tree.
findings.impact: Plaintext user passwords, API tokens and any personal data submitted through the action API are written into ordinary application logs and travel wherever those logs travel. This converts log read access into credential access for the accounts that happened to register or change their password during the window.
findings.recommendation: Do not log the payload. If a debugging breadcrumb is required, log the action name and the key names only, and pass the dict through a deny-list that blanks `password`, `password1`, `password2`, `apikey`, `token`, `reset_key` and `email` before any logger sees it. Apply the same change to the four Pylons sites so the two stacks do not diverge.
findings.preconditions: The `ckan` logger at DEBUG.
findings.verification: With DEBUG on, POST to /api/action/user_create with a synthetic password and grep the log for it.

triage.FP-01: DOES_NOT_HOLD - no field filter between the request and the logger
triage.FP-04: DOES_NOT_HOLD - shipped code, gated only by log level
triage.FP-07: DOES_NOT_HOLD - passwords and tokens are the payload

findings.title: Log injection through the action name in the API URL path
findings.evidence: `logic_function` is the URL path segment bound by the routes at ckan/views/api.py:509-514 (`u'/action/<logic_function>'`, default string converter). When the action is unknown, ckan/views/api.py:258 builds `msg = u'Action name not known: {0}'.format(logic_function)` and line 259 writes it verbatim: `log.info(msg)`. No allow-list or character filter stands between the path segment and the sink - the KeyError at line 257 is the only thing consulted. The formatter at ckan/config/deployment.ini_tmpl:258 is line-oriented.
findings.impact: An unauthenticated caller can forge log records by percent-encoding control characters into the path segment, with the same accountability consequences as EHS-A2-01. Reachable with a single GET.
findings.recommendation: Log with `%r` so the value is escaped, or restrict the logged form to characters valid in an action name before the call.
findings.preconditions: Requires the WSGI server and Werkzeug's path decoding to deliver a decoded CR/LF inside a single path segment. I established the sink and the absence of neutralisation by reading; I did not establish by reading that the decoding chain in the deployed stack preserves those bytes, which is why this is `probable` and not `confirmed`.
findings.verification: GET /api/action/foo%0aINFO and count the resulting log lines.

triage.FP-01: DOES_NOT_HOLD
triage.FP-02: DOES_NOT_HOLD - the value is a raw path segment
triage.FP-09: UNKNOWN - whether the server/Werkzeug path-decoding chain delivers a raw CR/LF into the segment was not established from the tree; this is what caps the status at probable

open_questions: Does the deployed WSGI server plus Werkzeug 1.0.0 decode %0a inside a path segment into a raw newline before routing? A single request against a local instance settles it.

findings.title: Stored XSS: markdown_extract strips tags with a single-pass regex and marks the result trusted HTML
findings.evidence: ckan/lib/helpers.py:1437 renders user text to HTML and then removes tags with one regex substitution: `plain = RE_MD_HTML_TAGS.sub('', markdown(text))`, where RE_MD_HTML_TAGS is defined at ckan/lib/helpers.py:2323 as `re.compile('<[^><]*>')`. The result is returned wrapped in `literal(...)` at lines 1439 and 1441-1449; `literal` subclasses markupsafe.Markup (ckan/lib/helpers.py:112), so Jinja will not escape it. `markdown` is the raw Python-Markdown import (ckan/lib/helpers.py:20), which passes raw HTML through by default. The character class `[^><]` excludes '<' as well as '>', so a tag whose attribute value contains a nested tag is never matched at its own opening bracket: for input `` the engine fails at the first '<' (it meets '<' before any '>'), matches and deletes the inner ``, and emits `` - a live element in a string marked safe. The codebase's own accepted sanitiser is bleach: the sibling helper render_markdown at ckan/lib/helpers.py:2382-2385 applies BOTH the same regex AND `bleach_clean(..., tags=MARKDOWN_TAGS, attributes=MARKDOWN_ATTRIBUTES)`. markdown_extract applies only the regex. That asymmetry inside one file is the evidence that the regex was never intended to stand alone. The inputs are unvalidated free text: `notes` is `[ignore_missing, unicode_safe]` (ckan/logic/schema.py:20) and group/organization `description` likewise. Callers render it site-wide: ckan/templates/snippets/package_item.html:19, ckan/templates/snippets/organization.html:44, ckan/templates/snippets/group.html:22, ckan/templates/group/snippets/info.html:23, ckan/templates/organization/bulk_process.html:68, and four more.
findings.impact: Any user who can create a dataset, group or organization - which on a default CKAN is any registered user, and datasets are public - stores script that executes in every visitor's browser on dataset search results, group pages and organization pages. Because there is no CSP and no other mitigating header (EHS-A2-10), the payload runs unconstrained: it can act as any viewer who lands on the listing, sysadmins included, and can read the API key that CKAN surfaces in the authenticated user's own pages.
findings.recommendation: Route markdown_extract through the same bleach allow-list render_markdown already uses, applied after the last transformation, and only then wrap in literal(). Do not repair the regex - a single-pass tag stripper cannot be made into a sanitiser.
findings.preconditions: An account able to create a dataset, group or organization. No special role.
findings.verification: Store `` as a dataset's notes and read the rendered HTML of the search listing; the img must come out escaped, not literal.

triage.FP-01: DOES_NOT_HOLD - the only control on this path is the regex, and the sibling helper shows bleach is the project's own standard
triage.FP-02: DOES_NOT_HOLD - notes/description carry only ignore_missing and unicode_safe
triage.FP-03: DOES_NOT_HOLD - literal() is markupsafe.Markup, so the sink is HTML that Jinja will not escape
triage.FP-10: DOES_NOT_HOLD - no CSP exists to bound the impact

findings.title: Stored XSS: uploaded resource served from the CKAN origin under a caller-chosen Content-Type
findings.evidence: The download view streams the stored file and then overwrites its content type with a value taken from the resource record - ckan/views/resource.py:177-180: `resp = flask.send_file(filepath)` followed by `if rsc.get(u'mimetype'): resp.headers[u'Content-Type'] = rsc[u'mimetype']`. `mimetype` is a caller-supplied field with no allow-list: ckan/logic/schema.py:48 declares `'mimetype': [ignore_missing, unicode_safe]`, so resource_create/resource_update accept any string. The uploaded bytes are not type-checked either: ResourceUpload (ckan/lib/uploader.py:237-289) has no verify_type step, unlike the sibling Upload class which does have one (ckan/lib/uploader.py:202-234). Nothing adds a Content-Disposition: send_file is called with no as_attachment argument, and Flask is pinned at 1.1.1 (requirements.txt:19), whose send_file adds no disposition header when as_attachment is false. There is no X-Content-Type-Options and no CSP anywhere in the tree - a grep for nosniff/Content-Security-Policy/X-Frame-Options over ckan/ and ckanext/ returns nothing.
findings.impact: A user who can add a resource uploads a file whose bytes are HTML, sets `mimetype` to text/html, and CKAN serves it inline from its own origin at /dataset/<id>/resource/<rid>/download/<name>. The script runs in the CKAN origin against any visitor who opens the resource, with no CSP to bound it - session-scoped actions as the victim, and API-key theft from the victim's own pages. WEB-12's own exculpating condition for this shape is 'served with Content-Disposition: attachment and a fixed type'; this code does the opposite on both counts.
findings.recommendation: Serve uploaded resources with `as_attachment=True` and a Content-Disposition of attachment, and restrict the honoured Content-Type to a server-side allow-list rather than the stored value; where inline rendering is genuinely needed, serve it from a separate origin. Add X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff globally (see EHS-A2-10). Constrain the `mimetype` field at ckan/logic/schema.py:48 to a known-type validator.
findings.preconditions: An account able to create a resource on a dataset. Default CKAN allows self-registration and public datasets.
findings.verification: Upload a file containing `<svg onload=window.__xss=1>`, set mimetype to text/html, and fetch the download URL; inspect the response headers for Content-Type and Content-Disposition.

triage.FP-01: DOES_NOT_HOLD - no disposition header, no nosniff, no CSP, no type allow-list
triage.FP-02: DOES_NOT_HOLD - mimetype comes straight from the caller via the resource schema
triage.FP-03: DOES_NOT_HOLD - the response is served same-origin with an executable type the attacker picked
triage.FP-05: DOES_NOT_HOLD - hosting arbitrary files is intended; serving them as same-origin HTML is not

findings.title: SSRF: the resource proxy fetches any user-supplied URL with no destination restriction
findings.evidence: ckanext/resourceproxy/blueprint.py:39 takes the URL from the resource record - `url = resource[u'url']`, a field any user who can create a resource sets (ckan/logic/schema.py:14, `'url': [ignore_missing, unicode_safe, remove_whitespace]`). The only validation is at line 42: `if not parts.scheme or not parts.netloc: return abort(409, ...)` - a presence check, not a destination check. The server then issues the request from its own network position at lines 49, 55 and 69 (`requests.head(url, ...)`, `requests.get(url, timeout=TIMEOUT, stream=True)`) with no allow-list, no private-address or link-local block, no DNS re-resolution, and redirects left at the requests default of enabled. The response body is streamed back to the caller at lines 74-84 up to MAX_FILE_SIZE (1 MiB by default, line 16-18), and the upstream content type is copied onto the CKAN response at line 71. The route is ckanext/resourceproxy/blueprint.py:111-113, /dataset/<id>/resource/<resource_id>/proxy.
findings.impact: The attacker chooses the destination and reads the reply. That reaches the cloud instance metadata service (169.254.169.254) and with it any instance credentials, anything bound to loopback on the CKAN host - CKAN's own Solr and Redis among them - and the whole internal network behind the host, all from an origin that is trusted by internal services. Because the upstream content type is copied through at line 71, an attacker-controlled remote can additionally have HTML served under the CKAN origin, compounding EHS-A2-06.
findings.recommendation: Resolve the host and reject non-public addresses (loopback, link-local, RFC1918, IPv6 equivalents) before connecting; disable redirect following, or re-validate the destination after each hop; restrict the scheme to http/https explicitly rather than relying on which adapters requests happens to register; and pin the response Content-Type to a safe fixed value instead of copying the upstream one. An egress allow-list or a mandatory outbound proxy is the durable control.
findings.preconditions: The `resource_proxy` plugin enabled (ckan.plugins), plus an account able to create a resource. The plugin is shipped in-tree and is the documented way to preview off-site resources.
findings.verification: Point a resource url at a canary you started on 127.0.0.1 and request the proxy route; the canary receiving the connection is the finding.

triage.FP-01: DOES_NOT_HOLD - no allow-list, no egress policy in the repository
triage.FP-02: DOES_NOT_HOLD - the URL is a user-set resource field
triage.FP-05: DOES_NOT_HOLD - proxying off-site previews is intended, reaching loopback and metadata is not

open_questions: Whether a given deployment enables the plugin. The defect is in the shipped code either way.

findings.title: JSONP on the util API executes with the caller's session, while the action API strips it in the same file
findings.evidence: The JSONP wrapper is applied in the shared responder: ckan/views/api.py:81-86 wraps any 200 GET carrying `?callback=` and re-labels the response `application/javascript` (`callback = html.escape(request.args[u'callback'])`, then `_wrap_jsonp` at line 146). The action API deliberately de-authenticates such requests - ckan/views/api.py:292-297: `if u'callback' in request_data: del request_data[u'callback']; g.user = None; g.userobj = None; context[u'user'] = None; context[u'auth_user_obj'] = None`. The util views reach the same wrapper and never do this: dataset_autocomplete (line 374), user_autocomplete (line 432), tag/format/group/organization_autocomplete (lines 391, 414, 447, 459) all call `_finish_ok(...)` directly with the ambient session intact, and are routed at ckan/views/api.py:519-533. This is the asymmetry WEB-24 describes, and it is decidable inside one file: the gate is at line 292, its ungated siblings at lines 374-469. The affected data is not public by default in every configuration - user_autocomplete authorizes through user_list (ckan/logic/auth/get.py:52-53 -> :80-88), which restricts to authenticated callers when `ckan.auth.public_user_details` is false, and package_autocomplete returns datasets scoped to the requesting user, private ones included.
findings.impact: Any third-party page can embed `<script src="https://ckan/api/util/dataset/autocomplete?incomplete=a&callback=steal">`; the browser attaches the victim's auth_tkt cookie, CKAN answers as the victim, and the attacker's callback receives the result. That leaks the victim's private dataset titles and, on a deployment with public_user_details off, the user directory - to any site the victim visits. The site's only ambient-credential defence is SameSite=Lax on auth_tkt (ckan/lib/repoze_plugins/auth_tkt.py:99), which does not restrict a script-tag GET.
findings.recommendation: Apply the de-authentication that already exists at ckan/views/api.py:292-297 in `_finish` itself, so every JSONP-wrapped response is anonymous regardless of which view produced it - or drop JSONP entirely in favour of CORS, which is already configurable (ckan/views/__init__.py:70-95).
findings.preconditions: A victim with an active CKAN session visiting an attacker-controlled page.
findings.verification: Authenticate, then request /api/util/dataset/autocomplete?incomplete=x&callback=cb from a different origin via a script tag and observe whether the response reflects the authenticated result set.

triage.FP-01: DOES_NOT_HOLD - the compensating control exists but only on the sibling path
triage.FP-06: DOES_NOT_HOLD - the second principal is the attacker's origin reading the victim's data
triage.FP-07: DOES_NOT_HOLD - private dataset titles and, in the restricted configuration, the user directory

findings.title: csrf_input() is an inert control: no CSRF token is generated, emitted or verified anywhere
findings.evidence: ckan/lib/helpers.py:3030-3031 registers a core template helper whose entire body is `return ''`: a control named for a decision that has no branch which returns anything. It has no callers: a grep for csrf_input and csrf_token across ckan/templates/, ckan/lib/ and ckan/views/ returns only the definition itself. No token is generated, none is emitted into a form, and no view or middleware validates one - a search for csrf/CSRF across ckan/ and ckanext/ produces no verification code at all. State-changing requests are therefore authorized solely by the ambient auth_tkt cookie. The one real mitigation is that cookie's SameSite default of `lax` (ckan/lib/repoze_plugins/auth_tkt.py:99), which is configurable and can be set to `none`.
findings.impact: The site's CSRF posture rests entirely on a cookie attribute an operator can switch off, and the helper's existence makes the control look present to anyone reviewing the templates. SameSite=Lax does not cover a state-changing GET, and any endpoint reachable by GET that changes state is exposed today; setting who.samesite=none exposes every POST. This is the shape WEB-27 warns about: an inert control that deletes findings rather than adding one, because a reviewer answering FP-01 will name it.
findings.recommendation: Either implement the control - generate a per-session token, emit it through this helper, and verify it in a before_request that fails closed for unsafe methods - or delete the helper so nothing reads as a control that is not one. Leaving a stub named csrf_input is the worst of the three options.
findings.preconditions: None for the reviewer-deception impact. Exploitation of the CSRF itself additionally requires either a state-changing GET or who.samesite set to none.
findings.verification: The negative test WEB-27 asks for: replay a state-changing POST with no token and no custom header against a local instance; it succeeds, which is the finding.

triage.FP-01: DOES_NOT_HOLD - SameSite=lax is a partial and configurable mitigation, not the control this helper names
triage.FP-04: DOES_NOT_HOLD - the helper is registered in the shipped core helper set
triage.FP-09: DOES_NOT_HOLD - the body is one return of an empty string; there is no benign reading
triage.FP-10: DOES_NOT_HOLD - the pack is explicit that a failed control is not a hardening note

findings.title: No security response headers are set anywhere: no nosniff, no CSP, no X-Frame-Options
findings.evidence: A case-insensitive search for X-Content-Type-Options, Content-Security-Policy, X-Frame-Options, Strict-Transport-Security, nosniff, SAMEORIGIN and Referrer-Policy across ckan/, ckanext/ and the shipped .ini files returns nothing. The only response-header hooks are ckan/views/__init__.py:70-95 (CORS) and :98-116 (cache control), registered at ckan/config/middleware/flask_app.py:216-217; neither sets a protective header.
findings.impact: This is the amplifier that makes EHS-A2-05 and EHS-A2-06 as severe as they are. Without nosniff, a response whose declared type is wrong can still be sniffed into HTML; without a CSP, an injected script runs unconstrained; without frame-ancestors or X-Frame-Options, authenticated pages can be framed for clickjacking, which matters more than usual given EHS-A2-09.
findings.recommendation: Add an after_request that sets X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff and X-Frame-Options/frame-ancestors on every response, and introduce a Content-Security-Policy - report-only first, then enforcing - so that an XSS in the markdown or upload paths is bounded rather than total.
findings.preconditions: None.
findings.verification: curl -sI any route on a local instance and inspect the response headers.

triage.FP-08: UNKNOWN - a deployment could add these at a reverse proxy, but no such artifact is in this tree, and the pack is explicit that 'the platform takes care of it' without the artifact is UNKNOWN, never HOLDS
triage.FP-10: DOES_NOT_HOLD as a standalone downgrade, because two confirmed XSS findings in this same report depend on the absence

open_questions: Whether the reference deployment sets these at nginx. No nginx configuration ships in this tree, so it cannot be answered from what I was given.

findings.title: rating_create never calls its authorization function, and the auth audit fires only after the write has committed
findings.evidence: An AST walk over ckan/logic/action/*.py for public action functions containing no check_access call returns rating_create among the few real hits (the group/org entries in the same list delegate to helpers that do check - _group_or_org_show at get.py:1153, _group_or_org_delete at delete.py:383, _group_or_org_purge at delete.py:497, _group_or_org_update at update.py:645 - and the follow/unfollow entries self-enforce at create.py:1359-1366). rating_create is different: an authorization function for it exists at ckan/logic/auth/create.py:131-132, whose own comment reads `# No authz check in the logic function`, and the action body (create.py:935-984) never calls `_check_access`. Every sibling action in the same module does. The framework's compensating mechanism is a post-hoc audit, not a gate: ckan/logic/__init__.py:529 pushes the action onto `__auth_audit` before `result = _action(context, data_dict, **kw)` runs, and only afterwards, at :538-541, raises `Action function {0} did not call its auth function`. By that point create.py:979-980 has already executed `package.set_rating(user, rating_int)` and `model.repo.commit()`. Additionally, when the caller is anonymous, `user = model.User.by_name(user)` at create.py:978 yields None and set_rating (ckan/model/package.py:490-531) falls to its IP branch with `ip = None`, writing a Rating row keyed on a null address.
findings.impact: The declared authorization for this action is never consulted on any request. The write commits and only then does the framework raise, so the caller receives a 500 that conceals a successful, unauthorized state change - and the audit that was supposed to catch this cannot prevent anything, only report after the fact. Concretely: unauthenticated rows written into the rating table, with no rate limit (EHS-A2-16) to bound the volume, and ratings feed the dataset ordering surfaced to every visitor.
findings.recommendation: Call `_check_access('rating_create', context, data_dict)` at the top of create.py:935 as every sibling action does, and decide deliberately whether ckan/logic/auth/create.py:131 should keep returning success. Separately, move the auth audit so it fails before the action's side effects rather than after the commit - an audit that runs post-commit is a detector, not a control.
findings.preconditions: None for the write itself.
findings.verification: POST /api/action/rating_create anonymously with a valid package and a JSON integer rating, then query the rating table. A row present alongside a 500 response is the finding.

triage.FP-01: DOES_NOT_HOLD - the auth audit is post-commit, so it is not a layer that cannot be skipped; it does not prevent the effect
triage.FP-05: DOES_NOT_HOLD - the auth function exists, so open access was not the declared intent of the API surface
triage.FP-06: DOES_NOT_HOLD - the second principal is every visitor who sees the affected ordering

findings.title: Rating range check is applied to the unconverted value, not to the converted one
findings.evidence: create.py:965 converts the input - `rating_int = int(rating)` - and then create.py:970 checks the bound against the *unconverted* variable: `if rating < model.MIN_RATING or rating > model.MAX_RATING:`, where MIN_RATING and MAX_RATING are floats (ckan/model/rating.py:15-16). The value that is actually stored is rating_int (create.py:979). When the action API delivers form-encoded data, every value is a string (`mixed()` at ckan/views/api.py:171-178), so the comparison is str against float, which raises TypeError in Python 3 and is not caught by any handler in the action - it surfaces at the generic `except Exception` in ckan/views/api.py:354-360 as a 500.
findings.impact: The stated bound is checked on the wrong operand, so the check either crashes or is comparing something other than the stored value. In practice a form-encoded call to this action is an unhandled 500. The range is enforced downstream by set_rating (ckan/model/package.py:518), which is what keeps this low rather than a range bypass.
findings.recommendation: Compare rating_int, not rating, at create.py:970 - and move the range into the action's validation schema so the bound is declared once.
findings.preconditions: None.
findings.verification: POST rating_create with rating as a string and observe the 500.

triage.FP-01: HOLDS in part - ckan/model/package.py:518 re-checks the bound on the float-converted value, which is why this is low and not a range bypass
triage.FP-10: HOLDS for the range aspect; the crash aspect remains

findings.title: Filename sanitiser is called and its result discarded in group and user dictization
findings.evidence: Two sites make the same mistake. ckan/lib/dictization/model_dictize.py:393-396: `image_url = munge.munge_filename_legacy(image_url)` assigns the sanitised value to a local, and the very next statement builds the URL from the *unsanitised* dict entry: `h.url_for_static('uploads/group/%s' % result_dict.get('image_url'), qualified=True)`. ckan/lib/dictization/model_dictize.py:541-544 repeats it verbatim for `uploads/user/%s`. The comment at both sites states the intent explicitly - 'munge here should not have any effect, only doing it in case of potential vulnerability of dodgy api input' - so the sanitiser is present precisely as a defence against hostile API input, and its return value never reaches the sink. This is the WEB-27 caller variant: the call sits on a line of its own with nothing consuming its result.
findings.impact: A user-set `image_url` reaches the generated static URL unfiltered. url_for_static (ckan/lib/helpers.py:493-506) blocks only a scheme or netloc, so path segments such as `../..` survive into the emitted URL, producing same-origin path confusion in whatever consumes image_display_url. The direct exploitability is limited - browsers normalise the result and sanitize_url (ckan/lib/helpers.py:1539-1568) re-quotes it on the one rendering path I traced - but the declared defence is inoperative at both sites, and a reviewer answering FP-01 on any future finding here would name a control that does nothing.
findings.recommendation: Use the sanitised value: build the URL from the local `image_url` the munge returned, at both model_dictize.py:394 and :542. If the munge is genuinely unnecessary, delete it rather than leaving a call whose result is dropped.
findings.preconditions: An account able to set image_url on a user or group via the API.
findings.verification: Set a user's image_url to a value containing separators and read back image_display_url from user_show; the munged form must be what appears.

triage.FP-01: DOES_NOT_HOLD - the named control's output is discarded
triage.FP-10: HOLDS for severity - the downstream sanitize_url on the rendering path bounds the impact, so this is low; the finding stands as a failed control

open_questions: Every consumer of image_display_url other than helpers.user_image was not enumerated; a consumer that does not pass through sanitize_url would raise this severity.

findings.title: Unauthenticated /_tracking middleware: unbounded body read, unhandled parse crash, and forgeable analytics
findings.evidence: The handler intercepts POST /_tracking in WSGI middleware, ahead of every CKAN authentication and authorization layer - common_middleware.py:70. Three defects in one block: (1) common_middleware.py:73 reads the entire request body with no bound, `payload = six.ensure_str(environ['wsgi.input'].read())`, and no size limit is declared or enforced anywhere for this path; (2) common_middleware.py:77 does `k, v = part.split('=')`, which raises ValueError for any body segment lacking '=' or containing more than one, with no handler around it; (3) the record written at common_middleware.py:90-93 takes `data.get('url')` and `data.get('type')` from that body with no validation and no authentication, keyed only on an MD5 of the User-Agent, REMOTE_ADDR and Accept headers (lines 82-88) - all of which the client chooses except REMOTE_ADDR. The SQL itself is correctly parameterised, so this is not an injection finding.
findings.impact: Anyone can (a) exhaust server memory with a single large POST, since the body is read whole into a string with no cap; (b) trigger an unhandled 500 with a two-character body; and (c) forge view counts for any URL at will, varying the User-Agent to defeat the de-duplication key. Tracking totals feed dataset popularity ordering and the search index, so (c) is a persistent integrity problem on what the site presents as usage data, not merely cosmetic.
findings.recommendation: Cap the read with an explicit maximum body size and reject beyond it; use a tolerant parser (parse_qs) instead of the unpacking split; require a session and validate that `url` resolves to a real local route before recording; and rate-limit the endpoint.
findings.preconditions: ckan.tracking_enabled true (registered at ckan/config/middleware/flask_app.py:358 and pylons_app.py:181). The middleware ships in-tree.
findings.verification: POST 'a' to /_tracking and observe the 500; POST a fabricated url= repeatedly with varying User-Agent and read the tracking_raw table.

triage.FP-01: DOES_NOT_HOLD - the middleware runs before any CKAN auth layer
triage.FP-02: DOES_NOT_HOLD - body and headers are entirely caller-chosen
triage.FP-08: UNKNOWN for the body-size aspect only: a reverse proxy could impose a limit, but no such configuration is in this tree

findings.title: Password reset key never expires and is compared with a non-constant-time equality
findings.evidence: The key is generated with adequate entropy - ckan/lib/mailer.py:210-211, `codecs.encode(os.urandom(16), 'hex')`, 128 bits from a CSPRNG - and stored in cleartext on the user row (`user.reset_key = text_type(make_key())`, mailer.py:206). Verification is ckan/lib/mailer.py:214-219, whose final line is `return key.strip() == user.reset_key`: a plain equality on a secret, not hmac.compare_digest, and with surrounding whitespace tolerated. Nothing carries an issue time: there is no timestamp field, no age comparison in verify_reset_link, and no expiry check in the consumer at ckan/views/user.py:703-707. The key is only rotated on a *successful* reset (ckan/views/user.py:748, `mailer.create_reset_key`), so a key that is issued and never used stays valid indefinitely.
findings.impact: A reset link remains a working credential for the life of the account. Any historical copy - a mailbox the user no longer controls, a mail archive, a forwarded message, a log or backup of the users table, since the key is stored unhashed - is a live account-takeover token however old it is. The `==` comparison is a timing side channel on the same secret; remote exploitation over HTTP is difficult, which is why it is not the primary impact, but it is the wrong primitive for a secret comparison.
findings.recommendation: Store the key hashed, record its issue time, and reject it past a short lifetime (an hour is conventional) both in verify_reset_link and at the ckan/views/user.py:704 call site. Compare with hmac.compare_digest. Invalidate all other sessions on a successful reset.
findings.preconditions: Possession of any reset link ever issued for the account.
findings.verification: Issue a reset link, wait past any plausible lifetime, and use it. Success is the finding.

triage.FP-01: DOES_NOT_HOLD - no expiry exists at either the mailer or the view layer
triage.FP-03: DOES_NOT_HOLD - the key is the sole credential for the reset

findings.title: No rate limiting or lockout on authentication; the failed-login counter is display-only
findings.evidence: A search across ckan/ and ckanext/ for rate-limit, throttle, lockout, max_attempts, failed_login and backoff returns exactly one family of hits, and it enforces nothing: ckan/lib/repoze_plugins/friendly_form.py:181-182 reads a counter and writes it back into the redirect URL (`failed_logins = self._get_logins(environ, True)`, `new_dest = self._set_logins_in_url(destination, failed_logins)`), and :296-306 parses it back out of the query string. The value is client-controlled - it lives in the URL - and no code branches on it to deny anything. The authenticator itself (ckan/lib/authenticator.py:16-35) counts nothing, delays nothing and locks nothing: it verifies the password and returns None on failure. The password-reset endpoint has no limit either (see EHS-A2-01), and neither does the action API. No brute-force protection exists anywhere in the tree.
findings.impact: Online password guessing against any account is unconstrained, as is enumeration and mass reset-mail triggering. This is what makes the counter dangerous rather than merely useless: it is named for the control and reads, to a reviewer, as though attempts were being tracked and acted on. WEB-03's own exculpating condition - 'attempt lockout bound to the identity and not only to the IP' - is absent entirely.
findings.recommendation: Add per-identity and per-source attempt limiting with backoff on the login, reset-request and action-API paths, failing closed when the counter store is unavailable. Move the failed-login count server-side; a counter carried in the URL is not state the server can trust.
findings.preconditions: None.
findings.verification: Replay failed logins against a local instance and observe that neither the rate nor the outcome changes.

triage.FP-01: DOES_NOT_HOLD - no enforcing layer exists in the repository
triage.FP-08: UNKNOWN - a WAF or reverse proxy could impose a limit, but no such artifact is in this tree and the pack forbids reading that as HOLDS

findings.title: X-Forwarded-For is trusted unconditionally as the client address
findings.evidence: ckan/views/__init__.py:136-139 prefers the client-supplied header over the transport-level address with no trusted-proxy list and no hop counting: `g.remote_addr = request.environ.get(u'HTTP_X_FORWARDED_FOR', u'')` and only falls back to REMOTE_ADDR when the header is absent. The value becomes the recorded author for anonymous actors at ckan/views/__init__.py:172, `g.author = g.remote_addr`. Nothing validates the header's shape or its origin. (The tracking middleware, by contrast, correctly uses REMOTE_ADDR at common_middleware.py:84 - the two disagree within the same codebase.)
findings.impact: Any client can dictate the address attributed to its own anonymous activity, so the recorded actor for anonymous writes is whatever the actor chose. Combined with EHS-A2-16 this also means any future source-based limiting built on g.remote_addr would be trivially evaded. Kept low because CKAN does not currently make an access decision on this value in what I read.
findings.recommendation: Parse X-Forwarded-For only when the immediate peer is in a configured trusted-proxy list, and take the correct hop rather than the whole header; otherwise use REMOTE_ADDR. Werkzeug's ProxyFix with an explicit hop count is the conventional fix.
findings.preconditions: None.
findings.verification: Send a request with a fabricated X-Forwarded-For and read the recorded author for the resulting anonymous activity.

triage.FP-01: DOES_NOT_HOLD - no trusted-proxy check anywhere
triage.FP-10: HOLDS for severity - no authorization decision currently reads this value in the code I covered

open_questions: ckan/controllers/ was not fully covered; a legacy consumer of g.remote_addr that makes a decision would raise this.

findings.title: CORS origin reflected without Vary, on responses marked publicly cacheable
findings.evidence: In the whitelist branch, ckan/views/__init__.py:81-85 copies the request's own Origin into the response - `cors_origin_allowed = request.headers.get(u'Origin')` - and lines 88-93 emit Access-Control-Allow-Origin along with permissive Allow-Methods and Allow-Headers. No `Vary: Origin` is added on any branch. The sibling hook that runs on the same responses, ckan/views/__init__.py:98-116, sets `response.cache_control.public = True` for every request not marked __no_cache__ (line 106). A shared cache keyed without Origin can therefore store a response bearing one requester's allowed origin and serve it to another.
findings.impact: On a deployment with a CDN or shared proxy in front, an attacker whose origin is on the whitelist can seed the cache with a response carrying their Access-Control-Allow-Origin, which is then served to other requesters - and conversely a legitimate origin's header can be cached and served where it should not be. Kept low because Access-Control-Allow-Credentials is never set (so the wildcard branch cannot leak cookie-authenticated data) and because the whitelist branch requires the operator to have listed the origin.
findings.recommendation: Add `Vary: Origin` whenever Access-Control-Allow-Origin is emitted, and mark any response whose content depends on the requester as private rather than public.
findings.preconditions: ckan.cors.origin_allow_all set with a configured ckan.cors.origin_whitelist, plus a shared cache in front.
findings.verification: curl -sI -H 'Origin: https://listed.example' a route on a local instance and inspect Access-Control-Allow-Origin, Vary and Cache-Control together.

triage.FP-01: DOES_NOT_HOLD - no Vary is set on any branch
triage.FP-07: DOES_NOT_HOLD - the cached header governs who may read the response
triage.FP-10: HOLDS for severity - no Allow-Credentials means cookie-authenticated data is not reachable through the wildcard branch

open_questions: Whether any deployment actually fronts CKAN with a shared cache. Not answerable from this tree.

findings.title: Session contents written to the log
findings.evidence: ckan/views/__init__.py:60 logs the whole session mapping when a session is about to be discarded: `log.debug(u'Session: %r', session.items())`. Whatever any CKAN extension has placed in the session - the session identifier itself, flash message content, any plugin-stored value - is written out. No filtering is applied. Same line-oriented formatter (ckan/config/deployment.ini_tmpl:258).
findings.impact: Session state reaches the log and travels with it. Bounded here because the branch fires only for sessions the code has already judged to hold no valid data, which is what keeps this low rather than a session-identifier disclosure across the board.
findings.recommendation: Log the session id's presence and the key names, not the values.
findings.preconditions: DEBUG on the ckan logger.
findings.verification: With DEBUG on, drive the logged-out branch and read the log line.

triage.FP-07: DOES_NOT_HOLD - session contents are not public data
triage.FP-10: HOLDS for severity - the branch only runs for sessions already determined to carry no valid data

findings.title: The snippet endpoint renders any ajax_snippets template with attacker-supplied template variables
findings.evidence: ckan/views/api.py:472-483 exposes /api/util/snippet/<snippet_path> (routed at line 526). Line 477 prefixes the caller's path segment with `ajax_snippets/`, and line 482 turns the entire query string into the render context with no filtering at all: `extra_vars = request.args.to_dict()`, passed straight to `render(snippet_path, extra_vars=extra_vars)` at line 483. The caller therefore chooses both which template under ajax_snippets/ is rendered and the value of every variable that template reads.
findings.impact: A caller can render any snippet out of its intended context and override every variable it consults, including ones the snippet trusts because its normal caller computed them. Whether that reaches a concrete impact depends on what the individual snippets do with their variables. This is not SSTI: the path names a file and the values are context, never template source - so ckan/views/api.py:483 is not an evaluation sink.
findings.recommendation: Restrict the accepted variable names to a per-snippet allow-list, and constrain snippet_path to an enumerated set rather than any file beneath the directory.
findings.preconditions: None; the route is unauthenticated.
findings.verification: Render each snippet under ckan/templates/ajax_snippets/ with hostile values for the variables it reads and check the output.

triage.FP-02: DOES_NOT_HOLD - both the path segment and every variable are caller-supplied
triage.FP-03: HOLDS in part - the value is context, not template source, so there is no expression evaluation; this is what caps the severity
triage.FP-01: UNKNOWN - I did not read every template under ckan/templates/ajax_snippets/ to determine whether any of them reaches a dangerous use of an overridden variable. That is what holds this at probable.

open_questions: Does any template under ckan/templates/ajax_snippets/ pass a caller-controllable variable to a sink that renders it unescaped or performs a privileged lookup? Enumerating those templates settles it.

findings.title: Database error detail - statement, parameters and driver message - returned to the API caller
findings.evidence: On a DBAPIError the datastore search path raises a ValidationError carrying the failing SQL and its bound values back to the client - ckanext/datastore/backend/postgres.py:1550-1558: `'statement': [e.statement]`, `'params': [e.params]`, `'orig': [str(e.orig)]`. search_sql does the same at :1617-1626, stripping only the literal 'EXPLAIN ' prefix via _remove_explain (:1618-1620) while still returning the statement, the params and the driver message. ValidationError is serialised into the API response body by ckan/views/api.py:328-335, so this reaches the caller as JSON.
findings.impact: Reconnaissance: internal table and column names, the exact generated SQL and PostgreSQL's own error text are handed to any caller who can provoke a query error. This is the finding that WEB-10's FP-05 moves to once the intentional datastore_search_sql exposure is set aside - the feature is meant to run the caller's SQL, but it is not meant to narrate the server's internals on failure.
findings.recommendation: Return a generic message with a correlation identifier and keep statement, params and the driver text in the server log only.
findings.preconditions: Access to a datastore-backed resource; a malformed query is enough to provoke it.
findings.verification: Send a query that fails and read the JSON error body.

triage.FP-01: DOES_NOT_HOLD - the detail is placed in the response deliberately, and ckan/views/api.py:328-335 serialises it
triage.FP-04: DOES_NOT_HOLD - not gated by a debug flag
triage.FP-07: DOES_NOT_HOLD - schema and generated SQL are not public information
triage.FP-10: HOLDS for severity - reconnaissance value only, no direct data access

findings.title: Upload size limit is enforced one chunk late, after the excess is already written to disk
findings.evidence: ckan/lib/uploader.py:28-40 increments the counter at line 32 before reading, writes the chunk at line 38, and only then tests at line 39: `if current_size > max_size: raise logic.ValidationError(...)`. The write therefore precedes the check by one megabyte-sized chunk, so a file of max_size + 1 MB is fully committed to the temporary path before the rejection. The temporary file is removed by the caller's except handler (uploader.py:187-189, :344-346), so the disk is reclaimed - but the write happens.
findings.impact: Each rejected upload still costs a full max_size + 1 MB of write bandwidth and transient disk before it is refused, and the limit the operator configured is not the limit that is enforced. Combined with the absence of any rate limiting (EHS-A2-16) this is a cheap amplification primitive for an authenticated user.
findings.recommendation: Test the accumulated byte count before writing each chunk, and count actual bytes read rather than loop iterations.
findings.preconditions: An account able to upload.
findings.verification: Upload a file of max_size + 1 MB and watch the temporary path; the bytes land before the ValidationError.

triage.FP-01: DOES_NOT_HOLD - no earlier bound exists in the tree
triage.FP-08: UNKNOWN - a reverse proxy body-size limit would bound it, but no such configuration ships here
triage.FP-10: HOLDS for severity - the temporary file is cleaned up by the caller
